idiom_name: typed view model + typed renderer contract (TSX element tree, react-dom/server, custom host config)
implementation_notes: TypeScript's contribution is the contract between the stages: the logical page is a typed model or props interface, and each renderer is a function with an explicit target type - (page: InvoiceVm) => string for a server HTML renderer, a component for the DOM channel, a custom reconciler host configuration for targets React never shipped a renderer for. React's element tree remains the logical presentation (TSX is type-checked, and react.dev describes the tree as platform agnostic), so the same page renders to the browser DOM, to a string on the server or to arbitrary primitives. Keep model types free of JSX and channel types, keep one module per channel, and validate data that arrives as unknown - a parsed JSON payload is not typed just because the interface says so.
pitfalls: A JSON payload typed as InvoiceVm is unvalidated at runtime: parse into unknown and narrow it, or every renderer inherits the assumption.
Typing props does not type the output, so a renderer can still emit markup for the wrong channel; keep one module per channel and test the produced string.
tsc catches structural drift between model and renderers but never escaping bugs - escaping is a runtime concern owned by each renderer.
